messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Mehta was 35 when he came for treatment, a married South Asian American man who worked as a tax consultant and had spent several months overseas as a relief worker in a war zone. He described one day there as the point around which everything in his life now seemed to turn. His team had been moving supplies near a densely damaged neighborhood when shelling hit nearby. He remembered smoke thick enough to sting his eyes and catch in his throat, the air carrying the sour, burnt smell of fire and debris. People were running in different directions, shouting names, crying out for help. There had been bodies and body bags later, and a burial area that relief workers passed on subsequent days, with fresh earth and grieving families gathered in numbers he still could not take in. What stayed with him most sharply was being down low behind partial cover, his body folded in on itself, his hands up over his face as he tried to protect himself from flying fragments and from seeing what was happening around him. He also remembered a man yelling—whether in panic, rage, or command, Arjun still could not say—and even now he reacted to anger in other people as if something dangerous were about to break loose.

When he tried to tell the story in session, the sequence kept slipping. He could describe the smoke, the posture of his body, the sound of shouting, the sight of mourners near graves, but he could not place these moments in a stable order. He would stop mid-sentence, frown, and say that it made no sense because parts were missing and other parts arrived all at once. When memories came up, he did not experience them as distant recollections. His shoulders rounded, his head dipped, and his hands rose toward his face before he seemed to realize he was doing it. He said that in those moments it felt as if his body were back there again, braced for impact. Just as strong as the fear was shame. He had come to believe that he should have protected people and failed. He spoke about civilians he could not reach and about the unbearable fact that he had survived while others had not. He did not claim he had had the power to stop a war, but he was certain he had fallen short at the moment that mattered most.

After he returned to the United States, these experiences followed him into ordinary life. He and his wife noticed first that evenings had changed. Daytime felt somewhat manageable because there was work, light, noise, tasks to complete. At night, however, he found it much harder to feel safe. Small household sounds made him jolt: a pan shifting in the kitchen, a car door outside, the thud of a neighbor on the stairs. He startled at sounds that he knew, rationally, were harmless, but his body reacted before thought caught up. Sleep became associated with exposure rather than rest. He would scan the apartment more carefully after dark and feel his attention narrow around possible danger.

His work as a tax consultant gave him a structured routine, but it also exposed the degree to which his concentration had changed. During client meetings he sometimes lost track of what a person had just said and needed them to repeat basic details. In the office, if someone spoke sharply—even a colleague expressing mild frustration about a deadline—Arjun felt his chest tighten and his attention break apart. Around tax season, when stress ran high and voices naturally sharpened, he found himself retreating to the restroom, standing with his hands over his face until he could steady himself. Smoke was another problem woven into daily life. The smell of cigarette smoke outside his office building, food catching on a pan at home, even a faint burnt odor from a city street vent could stop him in place and leave him momentarily disoriented.

Over the months he narrowed his world in ways that made sense to him at the time. He avoided returning to the relief site altogether and would shut down conversations if former colleagues mentioned the region. He also stayed away from funerals and cemeteries, making excuses when extended family or community members gathered after a death. He told himself he was sparing others his awkwardness, but he also knew that graves, mourning rituals, and grieving crowds brought him too close to what he had seen. More quietly, he began avoiding occasions that might have made him feel good. If his wife suggested a weekend trip, a celebration, or even dinner with friends, he often declined. Happiness felt wrong to him, almost indecent, as though hope would expose how little he had done for those who died. He had come to believe that the world no longer worked according to any dependable moral order, and that this left him cut off from people who still moved through life as if things were basically safe and meaningful.

By the time he sought help, the isolation had become hard to ignore. His wife had told him that she missed him even when he was sitting beside her, and he did not know how to answer. What finally brought him in was a recent incident after work: a coworker raised his voice in an ordinary disagreement, and Arjun flinched so strongly that he covered his face in front of everyone. He felt humiliated afterward and sat in his car, unable to concentrate enough to drive for several minutes because of smoke drifting from a nearby food cart. He came to treatment frightened that this was becoming his permanent life—that nights would always feel dangerous, that ordinary sounds and other people’s anger would keep reaching inside him, and that he would remain set apart from everyone he loved. At the same time, he said he was hoping, carefully and almost apologetically, for some way to remember what happened without feeling that his body was still there and without being crushed by the certainty that he had failed.
